summary.text: A telescope is a device for observing distant objects by the electromagnetic radiation they emit, absorb or reflect.
The first practical telescopes used glass lenses and were invented in the Netherlands, and designs that use mirrors followed within a few decades.
Today the word covers instruments that detect many parts of the spectrum, from radio waves to gamma rays.

facts.label: Word coined
facts.value: 1611, by Giovanni Demisiani, for one of Galileo's instruments

facts.label: Earliest record
facts.value: A 1608 Dutch patent filed by Hans Lipperhey

facts.label: Lens size limit
facts.value: About 1 meter (39 inches) for refracting telescopes

facts.label: First radio telescope
facts.value: The first purpose-built one began operating in 1937

items.prompt: Why have almost all big research telescopes built since 1900 gathered light with mirrors instead of lenses?

options.label: Mirrors were never affected by tarnishing
Lens makers stopped working on telescopes
A lens-based design cannot be built much bigger than 1 meter
Mirrors can detect radio waves and lenses cannot

items.explain: Refracting telescopes top out at about 1 meter across, so the large ones have been reflectors.

items.prompt: A team wants to study X-rays from a distant star. Where does their telescope have to be?

options.label: In orbit, above the atmosphere that blocks them
On a mountaintop, above the clouds
In a dark desert, away from city light
Anywhere on the ground, with a big enough mirror

items.explain: The atmosphere is opaque to most of the spectrum, so X-rays have to be observed from orbit.

items.prompt: A wavelength can be seen from the ground. Why might astronomers still put a telescope on a satellite for it?

options.label: Satellites are cheaper to build and easy to upgrade
Space telescopes can be made much larger than any ground one
The ground always blocks that wavelength completely
It avoids clouds, blurring air and light pollution

items.explain: Clouds, astronomical seeing and light pollution can make orbit better, though space telescopes cost more and are harder to maintain and upgrade.

items.prompt: You compare two telescopes, and one has a larger opening for gathering light. Besides collecting more light, what else does it give you?

options.label: A longer wavelength range
Finer angular resolution
Protection from cloudy nights
A lighter, cheaper instrument

items.explain: A larger aperture does not only collect more light; it also allows finer angular resolution.

items.prompt: An engineer must collect far-infrared light. How might the telescope work?

options.label: More like a radio telescope, using antenna technology
Exactly like a visible-light telescope, with simple lenses
Only by flying it above the clouds on a balloon
By ignoring mirrors and using only a camera

items.explain: Near-infrared can be collected much like visible light, but far-infrared and submillimetre telescopes can operate more like radio telescopes.

items.prompt: Early designers hoped a parabolic mirror would beat a simple lens. What did they expect it to improve?

options.label: No spherical aberration and less chromatic aberration
Less tarnishing and a higher size limit
Less spherical aberration and no chromatic aberration
A shorter tube and a lower price

items.explain: Parabolic mirrors promised reduced spherical aberration and no chromatic aberration, which led to many designs.
